extracted.intended_audience: novelists, fiction-writers, and literary students/critics studying craft
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the novelist's methods for creating believable worlds and handling the relation between pictured scene and dramatic action (how to prepare scenes, use background characters, control time, and temper romance/violence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Background characters must shed irrelevant life
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters who appear incidentally in a single story should not bring with them irrelevant past associations from other books; their only value is what serves the foreground action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a reappearing character's past belongs to another adventure and is irrelevant to the present protagonist, that past 'detracts' and 'disturbs the unity' of the story. Use only whatever of a peripheral character 'is of value for the purpose of the action in the foreground'; anything beyond that will lie idle or embarrass the narrative. Example/anti-pattern: Balzac's cross-book reappearances can confuse a single story if those characters retain unnecessary background detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain unity by avoiding distracting cross-references
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid setting up relations between incidental characters and the reader that obstruct the reader's view of the central character's world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not let known associations between a background figure and the reader (from other books) create a relation that has nothing to do with the foreground character; such relations 'disturb the unity of the story and confuse its truth.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare a pictorial scene as a 'reserve of vigour' for drama
rubrics_metrics.description: Before launching into concentrated dramatic action, provide a leisurely, detailed picture of the world that stores up force for the later action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A thorough preliminary picture (landscape, household, social world) gives the drama a reserve that helps subsequent action in multiple ways: it makes incredible events more credible, conveys duration, and lets the climax be lighter and more effective. Examples: Balzac's inventories; Dickens's gradual, well-populated approach in Bleak House.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use pictorial setting to temper overcharged drama
rubrics_metrics.description: When action threatens to seem harsh, overcharged, or romantic, employ pictorial description to qualify and make it seem more credible and less violent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberately reverse pure dramatic concentration by inserting picture-like material to 'rescue the power of his drama from becoming violence.' This tones down the effect so the story remains believable. Example: Dickens leads gradually into romantic climax through scenes full of character and humour to vouch for the later drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embed romance in a truthful background to disguise implausibility
rubrics_metrics.description: If plot elements are extravagant or romantic, ground them in a convincing background of social fact so the romance appears acceptable within the book's reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balzac attempts to 'absorb the extravagant tale into a study of actual life' so the falsity is disguised; success depends on the author's ability to create a background of truth. Anti-pattern: when romance remains 'staringly false' against a too-true background, the method fails (Balzac's occasional mismatch).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead violent or romantic intrigues gradually through populated scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce intense or mysterious action only after the reader has been immersed in a world alive enough to 'vouch for it'; gradual lead-in increases credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stevenson and Dickens exemplify this: populate scenes with characters and humour so that by the time the plot thickens the world is 'actual' and its air 'familiar.' Don't precipitate a fabulous climax without preparing the reader with a believable environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose between pictorial (survey) and dramatic (immediate) presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether to present material as a broad, pictured scene (summary, landscape of life) or as immediate dramatic action and dialogue; each method suits different aims and subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thackeray tends to general summarizing narrative; Dickens prefers scene and immediate action. The pictorial approach better conveys long-duration impressions and milieu; the dramatic approach is readier to work in action and dialogue. Pick the method that fits the subject and avoid using both in incompatible ways.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep imaginative stance consistent—avoid writing 'two books at once'
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not divide your imagination between incompatible modes (e.g., sober factual realism and gaudy romance) within the same work; such division weakens the book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balzac's 'passion for truth' conflicted with his 'lust for marvels', producing books where the two modes fight. Dickens succeeds because his imagination consistently assimilates both comic background and romance into one angle of relation to fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crystallize and label minor characters when using a dramatic presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: When many minor, scene-level characters populate a book presented as immediate action, render them sharply and economically—often by a vivid trait or label—so they function within narrow allotted opportunities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because such characters have 'few scenes' to act in, the novelist must sharply characterize them (sometimes via 'a trick or a phrase') so each appearance counts. Anti-pattern: attempting broad, reflective sketches for many minor figures in a drama leads to weak results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use first-person narration strategically to shift picture/drama balance
rubrics_metrics.description: First-person narration can push a work toward dramatization or toward a pictured impression depending on the subject and purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: In Esmond the first person raises the book toward drama; in The Master of Ballantrae it 'thrusts the book...towards the pictured impression.' Consider how the narrator's presence will alter reader perception of both action and setting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impose precision and fullness in physical description when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: A minute, inventory-like presentation of the scene (rooms, objects, architecture) can be essential as a preparatory condition for the story; don't be afraid of explicit detail if you truly 'know' the place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balzac's confident, business-like listings ('how the doorway is approached... the vases on the mantelpiece') work because he 'knows everything' about the scene; a less-possessed writer using the same mechanical sum of details would produce a lifeless account. Rule: only such precise plenitude that the author truly imagines will yield effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let the prepared picture supply sense of time and continuity
rubrics_metrics.description: A richly built picture of routine life and setting can secure the impression of elapsed time, so the narrative can summarize long spans without losing the sense of duration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balzac often writes 'Five years went by in this way' because his earlier picture (Maison Grandet, routines, household) already conveys the sameness and accumulation of years. Use environment, routines, and persistent impressions to imply long temporal stretches rather than forcing continuous interior narration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer external pictured presentation over introspective prolongation when character lacks interior richness
rubrics_metrics.description: If a protagonist lacks strong internal complexity, the novelist may achieve more effect by presenting their situation from outside (a pictorial, scene-based approach) than by prolonged interior focalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eugénie Grandet's character benefits from Balzac's external picture because her simple goodness lacks the inner material needed for a sustained consciousness-driven narrative. Anti-pattern: over-investigating a prosaic, good-natured character's interior can thin the effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let the climax 'only' perform its final organic task
rubrics_metrics.description: The climax should complete and unify the book—add the necessary final touch—without being burdened with tasks that could be (and should be) prepared earlier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare everything in advance so the climax need only declare and fulfil the book's intention. Balzac refrains from hinging Grandet on a sudden dramatic stroke; instead the climax is a pictorial impression of decay and loss. Anti-pattern: forcing the climax to achieve effects that were not primed beforehand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the physical stripping/denuding of scene to register cumulative ruin or repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: When a story depends on repetition (e.g., repeated failures), represent that cumulative effect through progressive, visible changes in the scene—furniture gone, house denuded—so repetition renews emotional force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In La Recherche de l'Absolu, Balzac shows Claes's ruin by gradually stripping the house; the repeated narrative shocks gain intensity because the visual scene manifests the damage. Use material, staged changes to renew rather than dull repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide whether to render facts 'by implication' in drama or to 'offer impression' by leisurely statement
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors must choose whether to make facts part of the drama itself (given by implication) or to present them in a deliberate, summary way as preliminary information; each has different effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balzac often 'offers his own impression of the general landscape...a leisurely display' before action; others (like Thackeray) summarize. Consider whether your subject needs the immediacy of implication or the solidity of declared picture.
